Immediate imaging will distinguish patterns (double bubble, multiple dilated loops, gasless abdomen) and help triage urgency. The most efficient next step is a plain abdominal radiograph (supine and upright) to look for air-fluid levels, double-bubble sign, and overall gas pattern before deciding on contrast study or surgery.

[THOUGHT] Neonatal bilious vomiting beginning within hours of birth, a distended upper abdomen with concave lower abdomen, tympanic upper abdomen, and abdominal radiograph showing a classic double-bubble (no distal gas) all point to a proximal duodenal obstruction present at birth. The most likely causes in a neonate are duodenal atresia (most common), annular pancreas, or rarely duodenal web, but duodenal atresia is the single most likely diagnosis given the presentation and radiographic finding. Associated anomalies (eg, Down syndrome, cardiac defects) are common but not required to make this diagnosis. Surgical correction is typically required urgently after resuscitation and decompression.

[DIAGNOSIS] Duodenal atresia.
